supplier_excerpts.quote:
Input: a finite expression DAG, a closed interval/rectangle domain box $X$, a
dyadic requested width $\varepsilon>0$, finite-format parameters, series
truncation index $N\ge1$, and integer total box-split budget $B\ge0$. Set a shared counter
$R:=B$ and a queue containing $X$. Process boxes in a fixed order. For each
box $Q$, evaluate the DAG by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] with the same format and $N$.

- If evaluation returns a non-finite status, return that status and the exact
  unresolved box $Q$; it is not a tolerance certificate.
- If it returns a finite enclosure $I$ with width at most $\varepsilon$, save
  $I$ as a completed leaf enclosure.
- If it returns a finite enclosure wider than $\varepsilon$ and $R=0$, return
  `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf hull, $Q$, and the unmet width test.
- If it returns a finite enclosure wider than $\varepsilon$ and $R>0$, select
  a widest nondegenerate input coordinate (breaking ties by the first
  coordinate in the input order), split it at its dyadic midpoint
  into two closed halves, decrement the shared counter $R$ by one, and append
  both halves to the queue. If no coordinate can be split, return
  `inconclusive` with the unmet width test.

When the queue is empty, take the hull $J$ of all completed leaf enclosures.
Return `certified(J,X)` only if $\operatorname{width}(J)\le\varepsilon$;
otherwise return `inconclusive(J,X)` and state that the global width test
failed. Each split covers its parent because the two closed halves overlap at
the midpoint and their union is the parent coordinate interval. The shared
counter makes $B$ a total split limit across the full computation.

For every finite input DAG and finite total split budget $B$, the algorithm
[[alg-budgeted-validated-range-evaluation]] terminates. If it returns
`certified(I,X)`, then $I$ contains the exact function range on all of $X$ and
has width at most the requested $\varepsilon$. If it returns `inconclusive`,
domain error, split-domain, or overflow, it makes no unconditional
tolerance-success claim.

The target value is $w=e^{\pi iq}=\cos(\pi q)+i\sin(\pi q)$ for the canonical Fourier $\pi$, identified with the interval evaluator's constant by [[thm-na-interval-pi-matches-canonical-fourier-pi]]. For precision $p=p_0,p_0+1,\ldots,p_{\max}$, build the finite expression DAG for $\cos(\pi q)$ and $\sin(\pi q)$, with rational constants enclosed by directed dyadic rounding, and call [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] with that precision and series cap; its fixed finite-cell rules govern range reduction. If $\epsilon\le\tau$, return `certified(\widehat w,\epsilon)`; otherwise continue or return `inconclusive` at the cap. A non-finite endpoint or overflow returns its explicit failure status. The routine makes no finite-error claim on a failure branch.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. At finite overflow, a directed result is
the corresponding infinite sentinel and its error bound is $+\infty$; the
status is `overflow`. The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of $\mathbb F$.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

Input: a finite expression DAG with real interval or complex rectangle input,
a finite dyadic format and an integer truncation index $N\ge1$. All constants,
including the Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the same fixed $N$ and format
throughout a call. Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure, or one of
`empty`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`, or `inconclusive` with the
unresolved domain piece. No value from a system `libm` routine is treated as a
certified endpoint.

1. Evaluate arithmetic nodes by
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. On an invalid divisor
return its declared status. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$; for
$\ln X$ require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. If an input is not wholly in the
stated domain, return `domain-error` rather than silently discarding points.

2. Set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$, using the exponent in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact dyadic comparison gives
$N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For an
interval $X$, evaluate the truncated exponential polynomial on $U=X/2^s$ by
interval arithmetic, add the symmetric tail using $\max_{u\in U}|u|$, then
square the resulting interval $s$ times. If its lower endpoint is not
positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or `overflow`. For
$\ln$, split $X\subset(0,\infty)$ into its intersections with the fixed
dyadic bins $[2^j,2^{j+1}]$. On each nonempty piece set
$Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$, $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$, evaluate the positive logarithm
series on $V$ with its tail determined by $\max|V|$, and combine
$j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Take the hull over all intersected
bins.

3. Partition $\arctan$ input at the fixed real breakpoints
$-3,-1/2,1/2,3$. On pieces within $[-1/2,1/2]$, use its alternating power
series interval evaluation. For $t\in[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; for $t\in[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t>3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Use odd symmetry on negative pieces.
Enclose $\pi$ by Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming their rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly
before the final outward conversion. If any branch test is unresolved, return
`inconclusive`.

4. For sine and cosine, first compute one outward Machin interval $P_N$ for
$\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, with the rational series endpoints
combined exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. For $k>K$, the outward lower endpoint of cell $k$ is
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its outward upper endpoint is
$-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus every cell enclosure that can intersect $X$ is
in the finite candidate list $-K,\ldots,K$. Use the fixed canonical cells
$[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$, $k\in\mathbb Z$. Enclose each cell using
exact rational expressions from $P_N$ and let $X_k$ be the interval hull of
its intersection with $X$; do not round candidate-cell or residual endpoints.
Include every cell whose $P_N$ enclosure cannot be ruled out as intersecting
$X$. Certify the residual enclosure $R=X_k-kP_N/2$ satisfies
$R\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the corresponding power
polynomial and add the explicit geometric tail by exact rational interval
arithmetic, then round the final endpoints outward. The tail comes from
[[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]], and map by the
quarter-period identities. Intersect every finite sine/cosine enclosure
with $[-1,1]$, including after the sign and coordinate swaps; the exact
values satisfy these bounds. If the input width is at least $2\sup(P_N)$,
return $[-1,1]$. If a cell cannot be certified in the reduced interval or the
finite candidate list cannot be resolved, return `inconclusive`. For tangent,
divide the sine enclosure by the cosine enclosure only on canonical pieces
where the latter excludes zero; otherwise return `split-domain` or
`inconclusive`.

5. For complex exponential, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$ and
$\sin(Y)$ and combine them by rectangle operations. For principal
$\operatorname{Log}$, require a rectangle excluding zero and every point of
the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`. Subdivide into
sign-stable quadrants and axis pieces; on the quadrants use
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\
-\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
For $x=0,y>0$ set $\operatorname{Arg}(iy)=\pi/2$, for $x=0,y<0$ set it to
$-\pi/2$, and on the positive real axis set it to zero. Enclose
$\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ by the real operations and elementary evaluators. If the
branch or sign cannot be certified, return `inconclusive`.

6. Each displayed series uses indices $0,\ldots,N$, hence at most $N+1$
terms; $N$ is the truncation index. Branch breakpoints, dyadic scales and
$P_N$ are fixed by the call parameters, independent of the input box; no
adaptive subdivision or precision refinement is hidden inside this evaluator.

Every finite enclosure returned by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for a real interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of that function on the represented domain.
If two input intervals are nested and both calls return finite enclosures,
the canonical branch-cell and fixed-term construction in the algorithm makes
the smaller interval's computed enclosure a subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

Every finite enclosure returned by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for a real interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of that function on the represented domain.
If two input intervals are nested and both calls return finite enclosures,
the canonical branch-cell and fixed-term construction in the algorithm makes
the smaller interval's computed enclosure a subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.
